title: ⭐⭐ Practice: reporting what was said, and describing what is changing

questions.prompt: Ian writes: "My wife is chatting to three people at once." A friend reports this the following week. Which version is right?

options.text: Ian said that his wife was chatting to three people at once.
Ian said that my wife is chatting to three people at once.
Ian told that his wife had chatted to three people at once.
Ian said me that his wife chats to three different people at once.

questions.explanation: Two things move at once: the possessive my becomes his, and the present progressive steps back to the past progressive, which gives was chatting. Keeping my leaves the reader thinking the wife belongs to the person reporting. told requires a person straight after it, so told that is not English — and a past perfect would step back one notch too far from a progressive. And said me reverses the pair: you say something, and you tell somebody something.

questions.prompt: Which sentence keeps the present tense correctly in reported speech?

options.text: He said that he is very tired yesterday evening.
He said that water boils at a hundred degrees.
He said that he is going to the cinema last night.
He said that the train is late this morning, but it arrived.

questions.explanation: A permanent truth does not stop being true when it is reported, so English is free to keep the present: water boils at a hundred degrees whatever day it is quoted. Being tired yesterday evening is a passing state, tied to a moment that has gone, so it needs was. Going to the cinema last night is the same case, and the words last night contradict the present tense outright. And the train that is late but arrived describes a state the sentence itself declares finished, which is exactly when the backshift becomes obligatory.

questions.prompt: The recording says the fingers of future man will be used a great deal. What does it predict for them?

options.text: They will grow less and less sensitive.
They will stay exactly as they are now.
They will grow more and more sensitive.
They will grow shorter and weaker.

questions.explanation: The passage sets up a simple rule and applies it twice: what is used develops, what is not used weakens. Fingers are used a great deal in modern life, so they become more and more sensitive, while arms and legs, used less and less, become less and less powerful. Predicting the opposite for the fingers is exactly the false statement your book puts in its true-or-false exercise. Saying nothing changes contradicts the whole argument, which rests on man changing all the time. And shorter and weaker fingers would follow the rule that applies to the limbs, not the one that applies to the hands.

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses the gradual-change structure correctly?

options.text: The nights are getting more and more longer.
The nights are getting the longer the longer.
The nights are getting more long and more long.
The nights are getting longer and longer.

questions.explanation: long is a short adjective, so it takes the ending -er twice: longer and longer. Adding more in front of a word that already carries -er doubles the comparative, which English never allows. Writing more long twice avoids that particular error but breaks the other rule, since a one-syllable adjective forms its comparative with the ending and not with more. And the doubled the belongs to the structure that ties two changes together, which needs a second clause the sentence does not have.

questions.prompt: Read this line from Janet's message: "If I spend hours on the phone, I'm seen as sociable; if I spend them online, I'm a geek out of touch with real life." What is she arguing?

options.text: That people judge the two the same way.
That online conversation is better than talking on the telephone.
That the difference in judgement is an irrational prejudice.
That she should spend fewer hours on the telephone.

questions.explanation: Janet sets the two situations side by side precisely because the hours are the same and only the judgement differs, and she calls that difference an irrational prejudice that a technologically advanced age should have left behind. Saying people judge them the same way denies the contrast on which her whole message is built. She does not claim that one is better than the other either; her request is that communication be valued in all its forms. And she never suggests cutting down her telephone hours, since the telephone is the activity nobody criticises.

questions.prompt: A pupil reports a promise. Direct: "I will help you tomorrow." Which reported version is right?

options.text: He said that he would help me the next day.
He said that he will help me tomorrow.
He told that he would help me tomorrow.
He said me that he had helped me the next day.

questions.explanation: Three things move together here: will becomes would, I becomes he, and tomorrow becomes the next day, since the day meant is fixed by when the words were spoken and not by when they are repeated. Keeping will and tomorrow leaves the sentence anchored to the original moment, which is what the shift exists to correct. told needs a person immediately after it, so told that fails whatever tense follows. And the last version makes two errors at once, saying me instead of telling me and turning a promise into something already done.
